event: Buildings assessed at 25% of value (to encourage building on vacant lots)
Improvements fully exempted (Mayor L.D. Taylor platform); continued each year to at least 1914
Changed from total exemption to 25% assessment of improvements

event: Improvement exemption fully ended ('scaled back over several decades and ultimately ended in 1984')
source_detail: England, C. (2018) 'Land Value Taxation in Vancouver: Rent-Seeking and the Tax Revolt', American Journal of Economics and Sociology 77(1):59-94, doi:10.1111/ajes.12218 (abstract via Crossref)

event: City charter (on incorporation as a city) exempts improvements entirely from taxation; poll, income, business taxes later dropped
Post-1913 land bust: 'Little more than half of the 1914 taxes have been paid' (city assessor letter Mar 16 1915); city facing first tax sales
Buildings assessed at 80% of value (first discrimination in favour of land)
Charter amendment: buildings assessed at 50%, to be cut >=10 points/yr until extinguished
Council cuts building assessment to 25% and raises land to 100%
Council 'change of heart': holds buildings at 25%, obtains charter amendment removing compulsory annual reduction; ratepayer vote required to raise building tax
Winnipeg assesses improvements at two-thirds of value by charter amendment; Manitoba legislature resists further moves
Building assessment reduced from 60% to 45% under Saskatchewan local-option Town/City Acts (gradual reduction permitted 1910-11)
Super-taxes on vacant land (Lethbridge; smaller BC municipalities); provincial 'wild land' taxes on speculative holdings in SK, AB, BC; Calgary doubled frontage charge on vacant property
By 1914 ~two-thirds of BC municipalities (incl. Vancouver, Victoria), all Alberta municipalities, ~a quarter of Saskatchewan municipalities had fully exempted improvements
source: IMF Staff Papers 1967 'The Taxation of Land Value'
